tx.t: In this talk I will explain what psychologists know about memory and how students can use it. In eighteen eighty-five, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus described the forgetting curve.
He found that people forget roughly half of new material within an hour if they do not review it. In nineteen fifty-six, George Miller suggested that short-term memory holds about seven items.
Reviewing material at increasing intervals, which is called spaced repetition, helps to move it into long-term memory. Testing yourself is more effective than simply reading your notes again.

tx.t: Today I would like to talk about the history of the Olympic Games. The ancient Games began in seven hundred and seventy-six BC at Olympia in Greece.

They were held every four years for about twelve centuries, until they were banned in the late fourth century. The modern Games were revived in eighteen ninety-six in Athens, mainly through the efforts of a Frenchman, Pierre de Coubertin.
Women first took part in the Games in nineteen hundred, in Paris. The first Winter Games were held in nineteen twenty-four at Chamonix, in France.
Today, thousands of athletes from more than two hundred countries compete in the summer Games.

tx.t: This lecture is about the short history of the internet. The first network, ARPANET, linked four American research sites in nineteen sixty-nine.

In nineteen seventy-one, Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between computers and chose the at sign for addresses. Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist working at CERN, invented the World Wide Web at the end of the nineteen eighties.

The web and the internet are not the same thing: the internet is the network, and the web is one service that runs on it. Google was founded in nineteen ninety-eight by two students at Stanford University.

tx.t: In this lecture I will describe the Aral Sea, one of the biggest environmental disasters of the last century. The Aral Sea, between Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, was once the fourth largest lake in the world.

From the nineteen sixties, water from the two rivers that fed it, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, was taken to irrigate cotton fields. By two thousand and seven, the sea had lost about ninety per cent of its volume.
The fishing industry collapsed, and ships were left on dry sand near the town of Moynaq. The exposed seabed is now a desert called the Aralkum, where salty dust storms harm people's health.
Today, tree planting on the old seabed and a dam in the northern part have helped to restore some of the water.

tx.t: In this lecture I will talk about the Great Wall of China. The wall was not built at one time. Different rulers built and rebuilt sections over more than two thousand years.

The first emperor of China, Qin Shi Huang, joined earlier walls together around two hundred and twenty-one BC. Most of the wall that tourists visit today was built in the Ming dynasty, from stone and brick.

A survey in two thousand and twelve measured all its sections at more than twenty-one thousand kilometres. It is a popular story that the wall can be seen from space with the naked eye, but this is not true.

tx.t: This lecture is about a successful conservation project in Fenwick Marsh. In nineteen eighty-five, only twenty pairs of otters were counted there.
The main reason for the decline was water pollution from farms. So volunteers and rangers fenced the river banks and cleaned the water.
By twenty sixteen, the number had risen to one hundred and seventy-one pairs, which shows that careful management can work.
